newsitem.title: USA: Accord reported on Mexico-drugs legislation.
newsitem.headline: Accord reported on Mexico-drugs legislation.

text.p: Senate negotiators and the Clinton administration reached agreement on Wednesday on legislation calling for Mexico to crack down on illegal drugs, a Senate source said.
The 11th hour agreement followed further concessions by senators to accommodate administration concerns, the source said. There was no immediate comment from the administration.
A major sticking point for the administration had been a provision that gave Congress a further role in assessing Mexico's progress in stepping up its anti-drug war.
An earlier draft had set the stage for a congressional vote on the adequacy of the response of both Mexico and the United States following a presidential report to Congress due by Sept. 1.
This provision was eliminated in the final version, the source said.
One potential obstacle remained to a swift Senate debate and vote on the legislation this week, probably on Thursday.
Democrats threatened to block all legislation in an attempt to force the Republicans to set a date for consideration of a chemical weapons treaty being held up in committee.
But an aide to Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said talks on this issue between Daschle and Republican Leader Trent Lott "look potentially promising," although there were no assurances.
Democratic senators will discuss how to proceed at a party caucus planned for Thursday morning.
Unlike a measure approved by the House last week, the Senate compromise does not overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico is cooperating in the anti-drug war.
Like the House version, it sets a number of goals for action to step up the anti-drug fight, but they apply to both Mexico and the United States.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat who was one of three senators involved in the negotiations, said: "This is a definitive statement by the Senate that the status quo is not acceptable and both countries have to redouble our efforts. Most assuredly we will review the progress in September carefully."

At a news conference earlier on Wednesday Feinstein and Republicans Paul Coverdell of Georgia and Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas warned the administration that failure to reach an accord would lead to a rancorous Senate debate and vote on a measure to "decertify" Mexico.
Feinstein predicted the Senate would defeat an unvarnished decertification.

The three senators and others had been in negotiations with high administration officials including Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin since last Thursday after the House of Representatives voted to decertify Mexico but suspend this action for 90 days to allow Mexico to improve its anti-drug performance.
The vote drew a sharp response from Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, who said his country's dignity and sovereignty were not negotiable.

The draft legislation calls for a series of reforms including strengthening of U.S.-Mexican cooperation and bilateral border enforcement, implementation of money laundering laws and eradication of narcotics crops.
